Tiers.title: Your results, your language
Tiers.subtitle: Whether you want the simple truth or the full clinical picture, you are in control.
Tiers.simpleExample: "Your glucose is a little high — think of it like your blood has more sugar than usual. It doesn't mean anything scary on its own, but your doctor should know."
Tiers.mediumExample: "Your fasting glucose of 112 mg/dL falls in the pre-diabetic range (100–125 mg/dL). This signals that your body's insulin response may be starting to lose efficiency."
Tiers.expertExample: "Fasting glucose 112 mg/dL (ref: 70–99). Consistent with IFG per ADA criteria. Consider HbA1c + OGTT to stratify T2DM risk. Review MetS components: BMI, lipid panel, BP."
Tiers.demoSimpleSummary: Your glucose is slightly elevated and sodium is on the low end — worth mentioning at your next check-up.
Tiers.demoSimpleSpecialistBody: Consider seeing an Endocrinologist to evaluate glucose metabolism and rule out pre-diabetes.
Tiers.demoMediumSummary: Fasting glucose at 112 mg/dL falls in the impaired fasting glucose range (100–125 mg/dL per ADA). Sodium is mildly low at 134 mEq/L — often dietary or hydration related. All other metabolic markers are within normal limits.
Tiers.demoMediumSpecialistBody: Consider repeating fasting glucose with an HbA1c to confirm glycemic trend. Review sodium intake and hydration habits with your Primary Care Physician.
Tiers.demoExpertSummary: IFG confirmed: fasting glucose 112 mg/dL meets ADA prediabetes criteria (100–125 mg/dL). Recommend HbA1c, fasting insulin, and HOMA-IR. Mild hyponatremia (Na 134 mEq/L) — likely euvolemic/dietary; reassess before pursuing SIADH workup.
Tiers.demoExpertSpecialistBody: Per ACC/AHA 2019: formal 10-yr ASCVD risk assessment indicated. Refer to Endocrinology if HOMA-IR > 2.5. Monitor sodium trend before adrenal workup.

About.missionTitle: Everyone deserves to understand their health.
About.missionBody1: You've just left the doctor's office with a printout full of numbers, abbreviations, and reference ranges. You're not sure if you should be worried. You're not sure what any of it means. And your doctor had eight minutes.
About.missionBody2: That gap — between the data you receive and the understanding you need — is what Meridix Labs exists to close.
About.gapBody1: Lab results are one of the most common touchpoints between a patient and the medical system. Yet most people have no idea what their results actually mean. A value is "flagged" but no one explains why. A diagnosis is given but the implications are never discussed.
About.gapBody2: Meridix Labs provides that missing explanation — not to replace your doctor, but to prepare you for the conversation. We believe an informed patient is a better patient.

About.value3Desc: We don't store your files. We don't sell your data. We never will.
About.value4Desc: We tell you what's there — calmly, accurately, and with appropriate perspective.
About.value5Desc: Whether you have a PhD or never finished high school, you deserve to understand your own body.
About.value6Desc: We help you prepare for your appointments, not avoid them. Meridix Labs is a starting point, not a substitute.
About.aiBody1: Meridix Labs is powered by Claude, Anthropic's AI model, which is trained to understand complex medical information and explain it clearly. We chose Claude because of its commitment to safety, accuracy, and nuanced reasoning.
About.aiBody2: Every interpretation is generated in real time based on your specific values. There is no one-size-fits-all response. The AI accounts for reference ranges, clinical context, and the specific markers present in your report.

LabAnalyzer.demoSubtitle: Three reading depths, flagged values explained, specialist guidance, an action plan, and supplement recommendations — all from one upload.
LabAnalyzer.demoSimpleContent: Your blood sugar is a little high and your vitamin D is low — both are common and easy to address. The good news: your kidney and liver markers all look great. Worth a chat with your doctor about lifestyle tweaks.
LabAnalyzer.demoMediumContent: Fasting glucose of 112 mg/dL falls in the impaired fasting glucose range (100–125 per ADA). LDL at 134 mg/dL is borderline-high (ATP-III). Vitamin D at 18 ng/mL indicates insufficiency. All three respond well to diet, exercise, and supplementation.
LabAnalyzer.demoExpertContent: IFG per ADA (FPG 100–125 mg/dL). Recommend HbA1c + 2-hr OGTT to stratify T2DM progression risk. Borderline LDL — formal 10-yr ASCVD assessment per ACC/AHA 2019. 25-OH vit D insufficiency: cholecalciferol 2,000 IU daily, recheck in 12 weeks.
LabAnalyzer.demoSpecialistContent: Endocrinologist for glucose metabolism and pre-diabetes evaluation.
LabAnalyzer.demoActionContent: HbA1c test in 4–6 weeks · D3 2,000 IU daily · 30-min walk after meals.
LabAnalyzer.demoSupplementList: Vitamin D3 2,000 IU · Berberine 500 mg · Omega-3 1,000 mg — full dosing & rationale included.
LabAnalyzer.demoResultSummaryHeadline: Your glucose and LDL cholesterol are mildly elevated, and your vitamin D is low — common findings that are easy to address.
LabAnalyzer.demoResultSimple: Your blood test shows a few things worth paying attention to. Your blood sugar (glucose) is a little higher than ideal — not diabetes, but in a range your doctor will want to track. Your 'bad' cholesterol (LDL) is borderline high, and your vitamin D is low, which is very common if you spend most of your time indoors. The good news: all three of these respond really well to simple lifestyle changes like diet adjustments, more sunlight, and exercise.
LabAnalyzer.demoResultMedium: The panel reveals three notable findings. Fasting glucose of 112 mg/dL falls in the impaired fasting glucose range (100–125 mg/dL per ADA criteria), suggesting possible early insulin resistance. LDL cholesterol at 134 mg/dL is borderline high per ATP-III guidelines (optimal <100, borderline 130–159). Vitamin D at 18 ng/mL is insufficient (optimal 30–100 ng/mL). Sodium is mildly low at 134 mEq/L — often a dietary or hydration issue. All other values including kidney function and liver markers are within normal range.
LabAnalyzer.demoResultExpert: BMP findings: (1) Impaired fasting glucose — 112 mg/dL meets ADA criteria for prediabetes (IFG: 100–125). Recommend HbA1c for 3-month glycemic confirmation, fasting insulin, and HOMA-IR to assess insulin resistance. (2) Borderline LDL — 134 mg/dL. Per ACC/AHA 2019 guidelines, formal 10-year ASCVD risk assessment is indicated before initiating pharmacological therapy in the absence of established ASCVD. (3) Vitamin D insufficiency — 18 ng/mL. Supplementation with 2,000 IU cholecalciferol daily with recheck in 3 months. (4) Mild hyponatremia — 134 mEq/L. Likely euvolemic or dietary; reassess hydration status and sodium intake before pursuing SIADH or adrenal workup given no other corroborating findings.
LabAnalyzer.demoResultEtiology: The elevated glucose is most commonly driven by a diet high in refined carbohydrates, physical inactivity, excess visceral fat, or family history of type 2 diabetes. Borderline LDL typically results from dietary saturated/trans fat intake, a sedentary lifestyle, or genetic predisposition (familial hypercholesterolemia). Low vitamin D is nearly universal in people who spend most of their time indoors — modern indoor lifestyles are the primary driver, with darker skin tone and higher body weight also contributing to reduced UV-B conversion.
LabAnalyzer.demoResultMechanism: Impaired fasting glucose reflects reduced peripheral insulin sensitivity or impaired first-phase insulin secretion from β-cells, resulting in insufficient suppression of hepatic glucose output after an overnight fast — the earliest detectable signal before frank type 2 diabetes develops. Elevated LDL reflects increased hepatic cholesterol synthesis or reduced LDL-receptor-mediated clearance; over time, cholesterol accumulates in arterial walls, initiating and propagating atherosclerosis. Vitamin D deficiency occurs when insufficient 7-dehydrocholesterol is converted to pre-vitamin D3 in skin via UV-B exposure, impairing downstream synthesis of calcitriol, which regulates calcium absorption, immune function, and insulin secretion.
LabAnalyzer.demoResultDiseases: Prediabetes / early type 2 diabetes mellitus (glucose elevation), Metabolic syndrome (glucose + lipid pattern), Familial hypercholesterolemia (if LDL elevation is persistent and family history is positive), Hypothyroidism (can raise both glucose and LDL — worth ruling out with TSH), Vitamin D deficiency-related fatigue, immune dysfunction, and long-term bone health risk. Note: These are educational possibilities, not diagnoses.
LabAnalyzer.demoResultSpecialist: A Primary Care Physician or Internal Medicine specialist is the ideal first contact — they can order follow-up tests (HbA1c, TSH, repeat fasting lipid panel) and coordinate referrals. If prediabetes is confirmed, an Endocrinologist or Certified Diabetes Educator may be helpful. If LDL remains elevated after lifestyle changes, a Cardiologist or lipid specialist may be consulted.
LabAnalyzer.demoResultAction: Schedule a follow-up with your doctor in the next few weeks. Ask about: (1) HbA1c to assess your 3-month average blood sugar, (2) Fasting lipid panel repeat, (3) TSH to rule out thyroid involvement, (4) Vitamin D supplementation dosing. In the meantime: reduce refined sugars, increase dietary fiber, get 20–30 minutes of moderate daily exercise, and consider a Vitamin D3 supplement with your doctor's guidance.
LabAnalyzer.demoResultSupplements:
**Vitamin D3 (2,000 IU/day with a fatty meal):** Directly addresses your low Vitamin D of 18 ng/mL. Cholecalciferol (D3) is the most bioavailable form. Take with lunch or dinner for better absorption. Recheck blood levels in 3 months.

**Omega-3 Fatty Acids (1,000–2,000 mg EPA+DHA/day):** Targets your borderline LDL and supports cardiovascular health. Fish oil or algae-based omega-3s have strong clinical evidence for lowering triglycerides and reducing cardiovascular risk.

**Berberine (500 mg twice daily with meals):** Has strong clinical evidence for improving insulin sensitivity and lowering fasting glucose — comparable to low-dose metformin in several studies. Discuss with your doctor before starting.

**Lifestyle (most impactful):** 150 minutes/week of moderate aerobic exercise. Even a 10-minute walk after meals measurably reduces postprandial glucose spikes. Reducing refined carbohydrates and increasing dietary fiber can improve all three flagged values within 8–12 weeks.

Privacy.title: Privacy Policy
Privacy.subtitle: Your health data, in plain English.
Privacy.intro: We wrote this policy to be readable, not just legally compliant. If you have questions after reading it, email us.
Privacy.sixtySecBody: We collect your email, name, and any profile info you choose to give us. We process your lab files with AI but never permanently store them. We use Clerk for auth, Supabase for your data, and Anthropic for AI. We don't sell your data. You can delete everything. That's the gist.
Privacy.s1Body: Meridix Labs is an educational health-technology platform operated by Meridix Labs. We are based in the United States. Our service helps users understand their medical lab results, symptoms, and diagnoses through AI-powered explanations.
Privacy.s2aItems: Email address and name (when you create an account)|Profile details you optionally provide: age, sex, medications, allergies, height, weight, health conditions, family history|Lab report files you upload for analysis|Symptom descriptions or diagnosis terms you enter|Goals, supplements, and notes you save to your account
Privacy.s2bItems: IP address and approximate location|Browser type and device type|Pages visited and time spent|Actions taken (button clicks, uploads, feature usage)|Crash reports and error logs
Privacy.s2cBody: If you sign in with Google or another provider via Clerk, we receive your name and email from that provider.
Privacy.s3Items: To provide and improve the Meridix Labs service|To personalize AI interpretations based on your profile|To send account-related emails (verification, password reset)|To analyze usage patterns and improve product features|To detect and prevent fraud or abuse|To comply with legal obligations
Privacy.s4Title: 4. How we store and protect your data
Privacy.s4Body1: Your account data is stored in Supabase, a secure database provider. All data is encrypted at rest using AES-256 and in transit using TLS 1.2+.
Privacy.s4Body2: Lab report files you upload are sent to Anthropic's API for processing and are not permanently stored on our servers. The AI-generated interpretation is saved to your account; the original file is not.
Privacy.s4Body3: We implement role-based access controls, so only your account can access your data. Our team cannot read your lab results or health profile without your explicit consent.
Privacy.s5Title: 5. Third parties we use to run the service
Privacy.s5Intro: We share the minimum necessary data with these providers:
Privacy.s6Body: We use essential cookies for authentication and session management. We use analytics cookies to understand how users interact with the platform. You can disable non-essential cookies in your browser settings. We use a locale cookie (meridix-locale) to remember your language preference.
Privacy.s7Title: 7. How long we keep your data
Privacy.s7Items: Account data: retained as long as your account is active|Lab interpretations: retained until you delete them or your account|Usage analytics: aggregated and anonymized after 90 days|Deleted accounts: all personal data purged within 30 days of deletion
